title: A curve family over a parameter: how does the curve move as the knob turns?
summary: Several curves of the same formula drawn on one pair of axes, one per value of a parameter. You see what the parameter does to the whole shape, not only to one number.

media.alt: Four curves y = exp(-p t) cos(3t) for p = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0, each with its own colour and line style, all starting at 1 and crossing zero at the same times.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How does the curve move as the parameter changes?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the independent variable t (here 0 to 6). y: the function value y(t; p). The parameter p is not an axis: it is carried by colour and line style, named in the legend.
look_at: What is the same for every curve? Start value and zero crossings are shared here: only the envelope changes.
What is different, and does it change smoothly with p? Compare the second peak near t = 2.1 for the four curves.
Are the parameter values evenly spaced? Here they are roughly doubled each time (0.2, 0.5, 1, 2), not equally spaced.
Is any member special (critical, optimum, boundary case)? A good family plot marks it.
as_drawn: Colour and line style both identify p, so the plot survives greyscale and colour-blind viewing. The legend sits in the empty top-right corner.
No member is highlighted. The taxonomy asks for a marked special p; this render leaves all four equal, so a reader cannot tell which value matters.
There are no units. y(0) = 1 for every p, which is a property of this formula, not of the plot form.
read_the_figure.proves: That the formula behaves the same way, qualitatively, across the plotted range of p. It does not prove anything about values of p outside the range, or about a value between two drawn curves.
if_wrong: Curves that cannot be told apart: colour and style are not used together, or there are too many members (more than about six) for the eye.
A legend order that does not match the vertical order of the curves forces the reader to hunt for each one.
Equal colour steps for unequal p steps suggest an even sweep that did not happen.

terms.meaning: A number held fixed along one curve and changed between curves. It is a constant of the formula, not a variable of the plot.
The set of graphs obtained from one formula by varying a parameter.
A smooth curve that the family's peaks follow. Here the decay factor that scales every oscillation.
A name written next to its curve instead of in a separate legend. It removes the matching step.
A parameter value where the behaviour changes character (critical damping, a stability boundary, an optimum).
How fast the output changes when the parameter changes: the derivative with respect to p.

remember: One curve per parameter value; the parameter is named by colour AND line style.
Same formula, same axes, same range for every member, or the comparison means nothing.
Mark the special parameter value; label curves directly when you can.
More than about six curves: switch to a colour scale with a colour bar, or to small multiples.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: x carries the independent variable, y the function value. Each curve is a line mark; the parameter is an extra encoding by hue (colour) and by dash pattern. Using two channels for one variable is deliberate redundancy: it keeps the figure readable in print and for colour-blind readers.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A single curve answers 'what does y do?'. A family answers 'what does the parameter do?', because the eye can compare shapes drawn on the same axes: which feature slides, which stretches, which stays fixed. Fixed features (here the zeros at t = pi/6, pi/2, 5pi/6) tell you what the parameter does NOT touch. In the render the parameter scales the amplitude by $e^{-pt}$ and leaves the timing alone.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Curves that cross each other make the order of the members hard to follow. Equal steps in colour suggest equal steps in p. A shared y range hides small members when one member is much larger. And a family drawn only for p between 0.2 and 2 says nothing about p = 20: the eye extrapolates what the data do not support.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: One colour per p lets you follow a member through crossings. A legend or direct labels let you read the value of p without guessing. A marked special p tells the reader where the story changes, for example the critically damped member of a damping family. This render satisfies the first two and omits the third, which is why it is worth asking what the special value would be.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For many members use a sequential colour map with a colour bar (a heat map of y against t and p is the limit of that idea). For two or three members, small multiples. To study one feature, plot that feature (peak height, zero spacing) against p directly.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Pick a special member (say p = 1) and draw it thicker with a label. Label each curve at its right-hand end. Add a thin dashed envelope $\pm e^{-pt}$ for the extreme p values to show what the family is bounded by.

steps.title: What stays fixed: the zeros
steps.note: The decay factor never vanishes, so the zeros come only from the cosine and do not depend on p. That is why all four curves cross the axis together at t = 0.52, 1.57, 2.62.

steps.title: Comparing two members
steps.note: At a peak of the cosine (t = 2 pi / 3 = 2.09) the ratio is the pure exponential. For p = 0.5 against 0.2 it is exp(-0.3 x 2.09) = 0.53; the render shows 0.356 / 0.659 = 0.54.

steps.title: Sensitivity to the parameter
steps.note: The sensitivity is the curve itself times minus t: zero at t = 0 (every member starts at 1), growing in size as t grows until the decay wins.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: Answer three questions from the figure only. (1) Which parameter value keeps oscillating longest, and how large is its second peak? (2) What do all curves have in common? (3) By what factor is the p = 0.5 second peak below the p = 0.2 second peak?

solution.text: The solid teal curve, p = 0.2, still swings visibly at t = 6 and its second positive peak, near t = 2.1, is about 0.66. The dotted p = 2 curve has a second peak of only about 0.02.
Every curve starts at 1 and crosses zero at the same times, 0.52, 1.57 and 2.62 for the first three crossings.
Ratio of second peaks, read: 0.36 / 0.66. Predicted from the formula at t = 2.09:

worked.answer: Smaller p means slower decay: p = 0.2 rings longest. The parameter changes only the envelope, so the zeros are shared, and the read-off ratio 0.54 agrees with the formula's 0.53.

analyze.q: The four curves have the same zeros. If a fifth curve crossed the axis at different times, what would that tell you about the formula?
analyze.hint: Think about which part of the formula the parameter multiplies.

analyze.q: Which members would you add to the family to show where the oscillation disappears entirely?
analyze.hint: Look for a value of p that changes the structure, not only the size.

analyze.q: Replace the legend by direct labels. What would you gain and what could you lose?

evaluate.q: A colleague says 'the curves are close together, so the model is insensitive to p'. What does the plot actually show, and what does it not?
evaluate.hint: The curves are close near t = 0, and sensitivity is -t y.

create: Redraw the family with p from 0.1 to 3 in ten steps using a sequential colour map and a colour bar, and compare it with this four-curve version.
Make a version that survives greyscale printing: which channels besides colour carry the parameter?

checks.q: What does the parameter p do to the curves in this render, and what does it leave alone?
checks.hint: Compare the peaks and the zero crossings.
checks.answer: It scales the amplitude by a decay factor that grows with t, so the peaks shrink at different rates. It leaves the starting value and the zero crossings unchanged.

checks.q: Two members with p = 0.2 and p = 1.0 are compared at a peak of cos 3t at t = 2.09. What is the ratio of their heights?
The family looks tidy, yet a reader cannot say which p is the interesting one. What is missing and how would you fix it?
checks.hint: Think of the third item in the checklist.
checks.answer: A marked special member. Find the parameter value where the behaviour changes (for a damped oscillator, the critical value), draw that curve heavier and label it directly.
